extracted.intended_audience: students, legal researchers, journalists, and general readers interested in First Amendment and press-law case history
extracted.subtask_description: Create or use a concise encyclopedic summary of a single U.S. Supreme Court case (facts, procedural history, holdings, and subsequent legal impact), emphasizing constitutional doctrine such as prior restraint and incorporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint on publication unconstitutional (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Near v. Minnesota ... is a landmark decision ... under which prior restraint on publication was found to violate freedom of the press as protected under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held that, except in rare cases, censorship is unconstitutional. Hughes: 'the fact that liberty of press may be abused does not make any less necessary the immunity of the press from prior restraint ... a more serious evil would result if officials could determine which stories can be published ...' This is the core rule: prior restraints are presumptively forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited exceptions to the prior-restraint rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The protection even as to previous restraint is not absolutely unlimited. But the limitation has been recognized only in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion lists example circumstances where prior restraint might be allowed: wartime statements that hinder recruiting or reveal sailing dates or troop locations; publications revealing 'crucial military information'; obscene publications; and speech that 'may directly incite acts of violence.' (Cites Schenck v. United States as illustration.) These are narrowly construed exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of the First Amendment against the states via the Fourteenth Amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the paragraph above cites the Fourteenth Amendment and not the First Amendment. This is because the Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First and makes it applicable to the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing state laws restricting press or speech, the Court applied the First Amendment through the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment — i.e., federal free-speech/press protections bind the states via incorporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard used by Minnesota: 'malicious, scandalous and defamatory' newspaper / public nuisance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Public Nuisance Law of 1925 ... provided permanent injunctions against those who created a 'public nuisance,' by publishing, selling, or distributing a 'malicious, scandalous and defamatory newspaper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Minnesota Supreme Court characterized a 'scandalous publication' as one that 'annoys, injures and endangers the comfort and repose of a considerable number of persons,' likening it to nuisances such as 'houses of prostitution' or 'noxious weeds.' This state-law test authorized permanent prior injunctions against newspapers deemed scandalous or defamatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: State deference to legislature for public-morals/public-welfare regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The court considered that a newspaper may also endanger safety ... Restricting the publication of a newspaper based on its harmful content accordingly fell within the legitimate power of 'the people speaking through their representatives' to preserve 'public morals' and the 'public welfare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minnesota courts gave heavy deference to the legislature's determination of what public interests require and what measures protect them. The state court viewed free-press guarantees as protecting an 'honest, careful and conscientious press' but not 'the defamer and the scandalmonger.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional analysis focuses on operation/effect of statute, not truth of specific charges
rubrics_metrics.description: We should add that this decision rests upon the operation and effect of the statute, without regard to the question of the truth of the charges contained in the particular periodical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court's invalidation of the Minnesota statute did not depend on whether the newspaper's allegations were true; rather, the statute's power to impose prior restraint was dispositive of its unconstitutionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-official libel standard (actual malice) derived in later jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) ... seriously limited the grounds upon which a public official could sue for libel. Statements made regarding their official conduct were only actionable if made with 'actual malice', meaning a knowing or reckless disregard for the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near was a foundational precedent leading to the development of the 'actual malice' standard for defamation suits by public officials, narrowing civil remedies and reducing incentives for prior restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodies and emotional-distress torts protected beyond the limited defamation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988) excluded parodies from even this limited standard, as they included no actionable statements of fact. Hustler made clear this protection extended beyond merely defamation suits to cover other torts such as intentional infliction of emotional distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later decisions extended robust protection to satirical/parodic expression and limited recovery under related tort theories where the speech concerns public figures and lacks factual assertions made with actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise rule often stated in summaries of the case-law
rubrics_metrics.description: No prior restraint of the content of news by the government is allowed unless it reveals crucial military information, contains obscenity, or may directly incite 'acts of violence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pithy formulation appears in the article's 'Basic case law resulting from this case' section and captures the standard exceptions courts recognize when considering government-imposed prior restraints on the press.
